conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and check on how you’re feeling. We’ll use the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Screen—better known as the EPDS. It’s a short set of 10 questions about the past seven days; it helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can sneak up after delivery, and it includes a question about self-harm so we can keep you safe. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me otherwise or there’s an urgent safety concern. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no numbers or letters needed. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, it’s felt kind of hard. I’ll still crack a little smile if something’s genuinely funny, but it’s like the joy fizzles out fast—like I’m too tired or foggy to really laugh. Most of the time I just feel flat or on edge instead.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, I can force a little chuckle when my partner shows me a silly meme or when the baby makes a funny face, but it doesn’t feel the same—it’s kind of hollow. I’m too worn-out and tense to truly laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try, but it’s like everything’s muted. I used to get excited about little outings or even just my favorite show, and now I think “that’ll be nice” but the spark isn’t there. A couple of times this week I managed to enjoy a short walk with the stroller, but mostly I feel like I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding him right or I missed some cue. Last night he wouldn’t settle and I kept replaying everything I did, sure it was my fault. I know in my head babies just cry, but the guilty feeling still sits heavy.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s fine, but my chest feels tight and my mind starts racing—what if he stops breathing, what if I drop him, what if I’m already ruining him? Nothing’s actually happening, but I can’t turn the “what-ifs” off. Sometimes I have to get up and check the bassinet three times an hour just to be sure.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, it hits out of nowhere—like this sudden rush of fear that something awful’s about to happen, even when the room is quiet and the baby’s sleeping. My heart races, I feel shaky, and for a minute I can’t catch my breath. It passes after a bit, but it keeps popping up a few times this week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is due, the laundry pile is staring at me, and I can’t remember if I’ve eaten. I keep thinking, “I just need five minutes,” but they never come. I manage to push through and keep the baby cared for, but I’m running on empty and everything feels heavier than it should.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I have trouble falling asleep almost every night. My thoughts just keep circling—worrying about the baby, replaying everything I might have done wrong, feeling sad and overwhelmed. Even when the house is quiet and I’m exhausted, I lie there staring at the ceiling for ages. Then I wake up once or twice with a jolt of anxiety and it’s hard to settle back down.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, that’s been my baseline this week. I wake up already feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest. I can still smile if someone talks to me, but the sadness creeps back in fast. Some afternoons I just sit there with the baby on my lap, tears welling up for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried twice this week. Both times the baby was finally asleep and the house was quiet, but instead of feeling relieved I just felt this wave of sadness hit me. I sat on the couch and the tears came—no single reason, just this overwhelming sense that everything is too much and I’m failing somehow.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it flashed through my mind a couple of times, like “what if I just wasn’t here.” I haven’t made any plans or anything—I could never leave my baby—but the thought popped up when I felt really overwhelmed. It scared me enough that I pushed it away fast.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels overshadowed by a constant heaviness: laughter is hollow, excitement is muted, and guilt arrives the moment your baby fusses. Most nights you lie awake with racing thoughts, and sudden waves of panic catch you off-guard. You're caring for your little one beautifully, yet you feel you're running on empty and sometimes wonder if everyone might be better off without you. These feelings are painful, but they don't reflect any failure on your part; they're common signals that extra support is needed right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can only produce a forced, hollow chuckle and explicitly states inability to truly laugh, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes diminished enjoyment ("spark isn't there") with only rare partial relief, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a lot" and gives a vivid example of repeatedly attributing the baby's crying to her own inadequacy, indicating this happens most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries about infant safety despite no real threat, consistent with "very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to find even "five minutes," and everything feeling "heavier than it should," which aligns with the highest level of inability to cope.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily sleep onset difficulties plus anxious awakenings, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness as a baseline, physical heaviness, frequent tears, and quick return of low mood despite brief smiles.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying twice in the past week, triggered by a pervasive sense of overwhelm and perceived failure—semantically aligns with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes fleeting intrusive self-harm thoughts ('what if I just wasn't here') occurring multiple times when overwhelmed, matching 'Sometimes</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places you well above the threshold indicating probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. You endorse low mood, loss of interest, excessive self-blame, daily uncontrollable worry, multiple panic-like episodes, and sleep disturbance, all persisting most days for at least two weeks, consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>. Question 10 reveals <sym>passive suicidal thoughts</sym> (<quote>what if I just wasn't here</quote>) without intent but warranting immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Contact 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline any time thoughts of self-harm return; if imminent, call 911 or go to the nearest ED
3. Share these screening results openly with your clinician so medication and therapy options can be discussed
4. Arrange practical support-partner, family, or friends-to handle night feeds or household tasks so you can rest
5. Practice 5-minute grounding techniques (slow breathing, naming five things you can see) when panic surges arise
6. Keep your next pediatric visit; ask them to help coordinate perinatal mental-health referrals if needed
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤12 wks after delivery (perinatal period)

**Symptoms endorsed**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia (Q1-2, 8)  
- Daily excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care (Q3)  
- Marked generalized anxiety & intrusive “what-ifs,” chest tightness, frequent reassurance-seeking (Q4)  
- Multiple sudden panic-like surges (Q5)  
- Overwhelming sense of being unable to cope, “running on empty” (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia: initial & middle-of-night awakening with racing thoughts (Q7)  
- Frequent crying spells (Q9)  
- Passive suicidal ideation (“what if I just wasn’t here”) without intent or plan (Q10)

**Pattern**  
Symptoms present “most days” × ≥2 wks; interfere with daily functioning and infant-care confidence; no periods of elevated mood or psychosis reported.

**Screening significance**  
High clinical concern for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety (possible panic spectrum).  
Safety: positive passive SI → immediate risk assessment warranted (current protective factors acknowledged; no plan).

**Next steps for chart**  
- Score and document EPDS (anticipated high).  
- Arrange same-day in-person follow-up / psychiatric triage for safety plan and definitive evaluation.  
- Provide 24-h crisis resources; instruct to seek ER if thoughts escalate or plan develops.
